write.desc: A short orientation tour of where single-variable real analysis leads: each point takes one idea from the course (completeness, compactness, epsilon arguments, the integral, power series) and shows what it becomes in a later subject, with one motivating example and no proofs, so the learner can see the course as a toolkit and choose a next course.

points.name: Constructing the real numbers from the rationals
points.what: The learner can explain in outline how the reals can be built from the rationals, either as Dedekind cuts or as equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences, and why either construction yields a complete ordered field, so the axioms used in the course are not an act of faith.
outside: completeness (least upper bound) axiom of the reals
Cauchy sequences and the Cauchy criterion

points.name: Metric spaces: the course with distance made abstract
points.what: The learner can state how convergence, open and closed sets, compactness, completeness and continuity are defined in a metric space using only a distance function, recognise the real line with |x - y| as one example, and see one new example (such as the plane, or a discrete metric) where the same definitions apply.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence
open and closed sets in the real line
compactness: sequential and open-cover definitions, Heine-Borel

points.name: Normed spaces and spaces of functions
points.what: The learner can describe a normed space as a vector space with a length, see uniform convergence as convergence in the sup norm on the space of continuous functions on [a,b], and explain why that space is complete while closed and bounded sets in it need not be compact, which is where Heine-Borel stops working.
outside: uniform convergence and the sup-norm view
Heine-Borel theorem (compact means closed and bounded)

points.name: Analysis in several variables
points.what: The learner can explain that in several variables the derivative becomes the best linear approximation (a linear map, the Jacobian matrix), why partial derivatives alone are not enough, and what the inverse and implicit function theorems say, with the circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 as the motivating example of solving locally for y.
outside: derivative as a limit of difference quotients
continuity and differentiability of the inverse of a strictly monotone function

points.name: Lebesgue measure and integration
points.what: The learner can explain why the Riemann integral is not enough (the Dirichlet function as a pointwise limit of integrable functions that is not Riemann integrable, and limits passing through integrals only under strong hypotheses), and what Lebesgue's idea of measuring sets and partitioning the range achieves, with the dominated convergence theorem named as the payoff.
outside: Riemann integral via upper and lower Darboux sums
Dirichlet function is not Riemann integrable
uniform convergence lets limits pass through integrals

points.name: Complex analysis: differentiable means analytic
points.what: The learner can contrast the real case, where a function can be infinitely differentiable without equalling its Taylor series (e^(-1/x^2)), with the complex case, where one complex derivative already forces a convergent power series, and can explain how complex numbers reveal why the real power series of 1/(1 + x^2) has radius of convergence 1.
outside: power series and radius of convergence
Taylor series and the smooth non-analytic function e^(-1/x^2)

points.name: Fourier series
points.what: The learner can describe how a periodic function is expanded as a sum of sines and cosines with coefficients given by integrals, and why questions about when this series converges (and in what sense) drove the development of rigorous analysis, uniform convergence and the Lebesgue integral.
outside: pointwise versus uniform convergence of series of functions

points.name: The analyst's toolkit and choosing a next course
points.what: The learner can name the recurring tools of the course (epsilon arguments, completeness, compactness turning local into global information, and justified swaps of limits) and say which later course (topology and metric spaces, multivariable analysis, measure theory, complex analysis, Fourier analysis) builds most directly on which tool.
